title: Free of three crooked things
hook: Mutta: free from the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband (Therigatha, Mutta)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punna, told to fill herself with good things like the full moon. Your line was a little more light each evening. What one good thing did you add to the day? Day seven hundred eighty-four.

Thud. Thud. Thud. A heavy pestle coming down into a mortar, pounding grain, the sound of a household kitchen in the Buddha's India. In the Therigatha, a nun named Mutta remembers that sound. She also remembers a man. And in a poem only a few lines long, she counts them up: three crooked things, and she's free of every one. Some of the nuns' poems are solemn. This one opens almost with a shout. Today, Mutta's poem.
screen: `THUD, THUD, THUD.` → `A MORTAR AND A PESTLE.` → `AND A MAN.`

segments.voice: First, the three. Mutta says she is freed, well freed, from three crooked things: the mortar, the pestle, and her crooked husband. The mortar and pestle were the daily work of pounding grain. The husband, the poem says plainly, was crooked. Why the tools are called crooked too, the poem doesn't say. Some readers think of their bent shapes, some of the bent back of the woman working them all day. Second, the same word. The poem puts the man and the kitchen tools under one word. It's sharp, and it's funny, and the Pali canon kept it. Third, the turn. Then the poem steps from the small freedom to the large one. She is freed from birth and death, it says, and what led her back into becoming has been pulled out by the root. The kitchen was a real weight. In the tradition, birth and death are the weight under every other weight. The poem names both, one after the other, in her own voice. Fourth, a kitchen as a doorway. Mutta doesn't begin with lofty words about release. She begins with the things that bent her back. The freedom the whole path aims at starts, in this poem, from something anyone could point to: a mortar, a pestle, a hard marriage. The poem isn't a verdict on kitchens or on marriage. It's one woman telling plainly what held her, and what doesn't anymore.
screen: `MORTAR, PESTLE, HUSBAND.` · `THREE THINGS, ONE WORD: CROOKED.` · `FREE FROM BIRTH AND DEATH.` · `A KITCHEN AS A DOORWAY.` · then, large: `SO FREED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one freedom you have. Settle, and let the breath move on its own. Look at your life as it is today. Find one thing you are free of, or free to do, that hasn't always been true. A job you left. A habit that loosened. A fear that shrank. A door you can open now. Name it plainly, the way Mutta named her mortar. You don't have to feel grateful on command. Just say what it is, and let it sit beside the breath. The bell holds the time.
Mutta. The nun whose poem says she is freed from mortar, pestle and crooked husband, and then from birth and death. Today's word.
Your line: so freed. Today, when you pick up a tool you don't love, a mop, a keyboard, a steering wheel, name the one freedom you found. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Mutta's short poem in the Therigatha is read by Buddhists and scholars as a frank voice from the early nuns, where freedom from household burdens opens onto freedom from birth and death.

notes: The Therigatha has two nuns named Mutta; this is the verse of the mortar, pestle and crooked husband (numbered 1.11 in some editions). Confirm the reference.
Paraphrase: 'so freed, well freed, from three crooked things: mortar, pestle, crooked husband; freed from birth and death, what leads to becoming is uprooted.' Confirm the second half.
The explanations for why the tools are 'crooked' are attributed to 'some' translators; confirm or cut.
The commentary describes the husband as a hunchbacked brahmin; omitted.
Name wordplay (Mutta / mutta, freed) stated as 'sounds like ... seems to enjoy'; confirm.
'In the Buddha's India' describing a household mortar and pestle: confirm it is not overreaching.
